Question 29
?

Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve x=z4+1 is rotated by 2π radians about the z-axis for z∈[−1,1].

a
2π∫−11(1+z4)1+16z8dz
b
2π∫−11(1+z4)1+8z6dz
c
π∫−11(1+z4)1+8z6dz
d
π∫−11(1+z4)1+16z6dz
e
2π∫−11(1+z4)1+16z6dz
Don't Know
Submit

decision.explanation: This tests surface area using the cross product of tangent vectors to a parametrized surface, absent from the supplied Linear Algebra topics, so it is prerequisite. Parametrize by r(z,θ)=⟨(1+z⁴)cos(θ),(1+z⁴)sin(θ),z⟩. The cross-product magnitude is (1+z⁴)√(1+(4z³)²)=(1+z⁴)√(1+16z⁶). Integrating θ over [0,2π] gives option e.

after.worked_solution:
Notice that $x={z}^{4}+1\ge 0$ for all $z\in [-1,1].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(z)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(z)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,(z,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(z)=1+{z}^{4},$ and

$$
D={(z,\theta )\,:\,-1\le z\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂z},\,\frac{∂y}{∂z},\,\frac{∂z}{∂z}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+({f}^{′}f)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(z)=1+{z}^{4},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}(z)=4{z}^{3}.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}(1+{z}^{4})\sqrt{1+(4{z}^{3})^{2}}\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}(1+{z}^{4})\sqrt{1+16{z}^{6}}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that x=z4+1≥0 for all z∈[−1,1]. The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

r=⟨f(z)cos⁡θ,f(z)sin⁡θ,z⟩,(z,θ)∈D

where f(z)=1+z4, and

D={(z,θ):−1≤z≤1,0≤θ≤2π}.

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

rz′=⟨∂x∂z,∂y∂z,∂z∂z⟩=⟨f′cos⁡θ,f′sin⁡θ,1⟩rθ′=⟨∂x∂θ,∂y∂θ,∂z∂θ⟩=⟨−fsin⁡θ,f(y)cos⁡θ,0⟩

Next, the fundamental vector product is

rz′×rθ′=|ijkf′cos⁡θf′sin⁡θ1−fsin⁡θfcos⁡θ0|=⟨|f′sin⁡θ1fcos⁡θ0|,−|f′cos⁡θ1−fsin⁡θ0|,|f′cos⁡θf′sin⁡θ−fsin⁡θfcos⁡θ|⟩=⟨−fcos⁡θ,−fsin⁡θ,f′fcos2⁡θ+f′fsin2⁡θ⟩=⟨−fcos⁡θ,−fsin⁡θ,f′f⟩.

and

‖rz′×rθ′‖=(−fcos⁡θ)2+(−fsin⁡θ)2+(f′f)2=f2(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)+f2(f′)2=f2+f2(f′)2=f1+(f′)2.

Therefore, the surface area is

A=∬SdS=∬D‖rz′×rθ′‖dzdθ=∬Df1+(f′)2dzdθ=∫−11f1+(f′)2∫02πdθdz=∫−11f1+(f′)2⋅θ|02πdz=2π∫−11f1+(f′)2dz.

Since f(z)=1+z4, we obtain f′(z)=4z3. So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

2π∫−11f1+(f′)2dz=2π∫−11(1+z4)1+(4z3)2dz=2π∫−11(1+z4)1+16z6dz.

decision.explanation: The differential is df=ln(y) dx+(x/y) dy. At (0,e), the partial derivatives are 1 and 0. With dx=1 and dy=2−e, the estimated change is df=1·1+0·(2−e)=1.

after.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,\text{d}x+\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(0,e),$ the differential is

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(4\pi ,8) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi \,\text{d}x+1\,\text{d}y \\  & =0\,\text{d}x+1\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}

$$
Δf≈0\,Δx+1\,Δy.

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =13-4\pi , \\ Δy & =8.5-8=0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈0\,Δx+1\,Δy \\  & ≈0\cdot (13-4\pi )+1\cdot (0.5) \\  & ≈0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y)$ increases by approximately $0.5.$

decision.explanation: For I and II, the integrands and their t derivatives are continuous and bounded on [0,1] in a sufficiently small neighborhood of each allowed t, permitting differentiation under the integral sign. For III, the t derivative has a nonintegrable |x−t|^(−3/2) singularity. Although F₃ itself is differentiable, direct differentiation under its integral sign is invalid. Thus I and II only.

after.worked_solution:
Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\times [c,d]$ and $\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function

$$
F(t)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x
$$

is differentiable on $(c,d),$ and

$$
{F}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\,\text{d}x.
$$

This is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*

With that in mind, let's check each function:

- For the first function, we have 

$$
{f}_{1}(x,t)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+tx)}{1+{x}^{2}}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (-1,1)$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(-1,1)$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{1}$ is continuous on $R$ (since $1+tx>0$). Computing the  partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂t}=\frac{x}{(1+tx)(1+{x}^{2})}
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{1}^{′}(t)$ for all $t\in (-1,1).$

- For the second function, we have 

$$
{f}_{2}(x,t)=\frac{1}{x-t}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (1,2)$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(1,2)$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{2}$ is continuous on $R$ (since the denominator never vanishes on $R$). Computing the partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂t}=\frac{1}{(x-t)^{2}},
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{2}^{′}(t)$ for all $t\in (1,2).$

- For the third function, we have 

$$
{f}_{3}(x,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|x-t|}}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (0,1)$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(0,1)$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that this function is undefined when $x=t,$ since the denominator vanishes. Thus, ${f}_{3}$ is not continuous on $R,$ and differentiating under the integral sign is *not* valid.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

decision.explanation: For I and III, the integrands and their t derivatives are continuous on [0,1] in a neighborhood of every specified t, so differentiation under the integral sign is valid. Question 34
?

Consider the arc of the curve x=y312+1y that lies between the lines y=1 and y=e. Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis.

a
 π8(e4+15)
b
 πe24
c
 π15(e4+1)
d
 4π15(e4−12)
e
 πe432
Don't Know
Submit

decision.explanation: This tests surface area of revolution, absent from the supplied Linear Algebra topics, so it is prerequisite. Here dx/dy=y²/4−1/y², and √(1+(dx/dy)²)=y²/4+1/y². Thus A=2π∫₁ᵉ(y³/4+1/y)dy=2π[(e⁴−1)/16+1]=π(e⁴+15)/8.

after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${y}_{1}=1$ to ${y}_{2}=e.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{{y}^{3}}{12}+\frac{1}{y})=\frac{{y}^{4}-4}{4{y}^{2}}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}=\frac{{y}^{8}-8{y}^{4}+16}{16{y}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}y\sqrt{1+\frac{{y}^{8}-8{y}^{4}+16}{16{y}^{4}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}y\sqrt{\frac{{y}^{8}+8{y}^{4}+16}{16{y}^{4}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}\,y\sqrt{\frac{({y}^{4}+4)^{2}}{16{y}^{4}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}y(\frac{{y}^{4}+4}{4{y}^{2}})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{{y}^{4}+4}{y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}{\int }_{1}^{e}({y}^{3}+\frac{4}{y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}{(\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}+4\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(\frac{{e}^{4}}{4}+4-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}({e}^{4}+15).\end{aligned}
$$

S=∫2πyds.

Since we're given a curve in the form x=f(y), we have

ds=1+(dxdy)2dy. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫y1y2y1+(dxdy)2dy.

We are told that the limits of integration are from y1=1 to y2=e.

Computing the derivative, we get

dxdy=ddy(y312+1y)=y4−44y2⇒(dxdy)2=y8−8y4+1616y4.

Therefore,

S=2π∫y1y2y1+(dxdy)2dy=2π∫1ey1+y8−8y4+1616y4dy=2π∫1eyy8+8y4+1616y4dy=2π∫1ey(y4+4)216y4dy=2π∫1ey(y4+44y2)dy=π2∫1ey4+4ydy=π2∫1e(y3+4y)dy=π2(y44+4ln⁡y)|1e=π2(e44+4−14)=π8(e4+15).

before.problem:
Find ${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t$ 
given that 
${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(t)\,\text{d}t=4\,i+2\,k$

The cross-product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the cross-product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\times {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(i+j-k)\times (4\,i+2\,k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 4 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(2-0)i-(2+4)j+(0-4)k \\  & =2i-6j-4k.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: This tests double integrals defined by lower and upper Riemann sums, absent from the supplied Linear Algebra topics, so it is prerequisite. Telescoping gives (L+U)/2=(6²−5²)(3−1)−(3/2)(3²−1²)(6−5)=22−12=10 for every partition. Also U−L=ΣΣ(2Δx_i+3Δy_j)Δx_iΔy_j tends to zero as the mesh tends to zero. Thus both sums converge to 10.

after.worked_solution:
For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P)\le I\le U(f,P)
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R.$

First, notice that ${\overset{¯}{x}}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})$ will always lie between ${x}_{i-1}$ and ${x}_{i}$, and similarly ${\overset{¯}{y}}_{j}=\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})$ will always lie between ${y}_{j-1}$ and ${y}_{j}.$ Therefore,

$$
2{x}_{i-1}-3{y}_{j}\le 2\cdot \frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-3\cdot \frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\le 2{x}_{i}-3{y}_{j-1}
$$

which simplifies to

$$
2{x}_{i-1}-3{y}_{j}\le ({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{3}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\le 2{x}_{i}-3{y}_{j-1}.
$$

Multiplying this by $Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}$ and applying the double summation gives:

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{3}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})]Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P)
$$

Separating the sums using the addition and constant multiple rules, we get

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}-\frac{3}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P).
$$

Using the hint, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =({6}^{2}-{5}^{2})(3-1)=22 \\ \frac{3}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{3}{2}({3}^{2}-{1}^{2})(6-5)=12\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)\le 22-12\le U(f,P)\,⟹\,L(f,P)\le 10\le U(f,P)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=10.
$$

Telescoping gives (L+U)/2=(10²−8²)(3−1)−2(3²−1²)(10−8)−3(3−1)(10−8)=72−32−12=28. Also U−L=ΣΣ(2Δy_j+4Δx_i)Δx_iΔy_j tends to zero as the mesh tends to zero. Thus both sums converge to 28.

after.worked_solution:
For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P)\le I\le U(f,P)
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R.$

First, notice that ${\overset{¯}{x}}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})$ will always lie between ${x}_{i-1}$ and ${x}_{i}$, and similarly ${\overset{¯}{y}}_{j}=\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})$ will always lie between ${y}_{j-1}$ and ${y}_{j}.$ Therefore,

$$
2{y}_{j-1}-4{x}_{i}-3\le 2\cdot \frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})-4\cdot \frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-3\le 2{y}_{j}-4{x}_{i-1}-3
$$

which simplifies to 

$$
2{y}_{j-1}-4{x}_{i}-3\le ({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})-2({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-3\le 2{y}_{j}-4{x}_{i-1}-3.
$$

Multiplying this by $Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}$ and applying the double summation gives:

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})-2({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-3]Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P)
$$

Separating the sums using the addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & \le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \,-2{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \,-3{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \le U(f,P).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the hint, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{j-1}+{x}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =2({3}^{2}-{1}^{2})(10-8)=32 \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =({10}^{2}-{8}^{2})(3-1)=72 \\ 3{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =3(3-1)(10-8)=12\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)\le 72-32-12\le U(f,P)\,⟹\,L(f,P)\le 28\le U(f,P)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=28.
$$

decision.explanation: Since y=r sinθ=cscθ sinθ=1, the curve is horizontal, so dy/dx=0 and d²y/dx²=0. This tests differentiation of polar curves, which is absent from the supplied Linear Algebra topics, so it is prerequisite.

after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{d\theta })}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ and $\frac{dx}{d\theta }.$ 

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

as parametric equations of a curve in terms of $\theta .$ 

Using the fact that $r=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ,$ we get

$$
x=\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ,\,y=1.
$$

Then, to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=0.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{0}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta }=0.
$$

Finally, substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(0)}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{0}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the formula

d2ydx2=ddθ(dydx)(dxdθ).

First, we need to find dydx and dxdθ.

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ

as parametric equations of a curve in terms of θ.

Using the fact that r=csc⁡θ, we get

x=cot⁡θ,y=1.

Then, to find dydx we use the rule

dydx=y′(θ)x′(θ).

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

x′(θ)=−csc2⁡θ,y′(θ)=0.

Therefore,

dydx=0−csc2⁡θ=0.

Finally, substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get

d2ydx2=ddθ(0)−csc2⁡θ=0−csc2⁡θ=0.

as parametric equations of a curve in terms of $\theta .$ 

Using the fact that $r=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ,$ we get

$$
x=\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ,\,y=1.
$$

Then, to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=0.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{0}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta }=0.
$$

Finally, substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(0)}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{0}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 41
?

Express z=6−1+i in the form r(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ).

a
z=32(cos⁡(3π4)+isin⁡(3π4))
b
z=3(cos⁡(7π4)+isin⁡(7π4))
c
z=32(cos⁡(5π4)+isin⁡(5π4))
d
z=2(cos⁡(3π4)+isin⁡(3π4))
e
z=23(cos⁡(π4)+isin⁡(π4))
Don't Know
Submit

decision.explanation: Rationalizing gives z=6(-1-i)/2=-3-3i. Its modulus is 3√2 and its argument is 5π/4, so choice c is correct.

after.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $-1-\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{6}{-1+\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{(-1+\text{i})(-1-\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{(-1)^{2}-{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{1+1} \\  & =3(-1-\text{i}) \\  & =-3-3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

 

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=-3-3\text{i},$ the magnitude is 

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{18} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

    

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=-3$ and $y=-3$ are both negative, $z$ lies in the third quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-3}{-3}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡1 \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=3\sqrt{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4}))
$$

before.html:
Question 42
?

Express z=−23i in the form r(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ).

a
z=43(cos⁡(π2)+isin⁡(π2))
b
z=43(cos⁡(3π4)+isin⁡(3π4))
c
z=23(cos⁡(3π2)+isin⁡(3π2))
d
z=23(cos⁡(π2)+isin⁡(π2))
e
z=23(cos⁡(π4)+isin⁡(π4))
Don't Know
Submit

decision.explanation: Since 1/i=-i, z=-2/(3i)=2i/3. Its modulus is 2/3 and its argument is π/2, giving choice d.

after.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $-3\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =-\frac{2}{3\text{i}} \\  & =-\frac{2(-3\text{i})}{(3\text{i})(-3\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{6\text{i}}{-9{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6\text{i}}{9} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

 

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=\frac{2}{3}\text{i}=0+\frac{2}{3}\text{i},$ the magnitude is 

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

    

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=0$  and $y=\frac{2}{3}$ is positive, $z$ lies on the positive direction of the $y$-axis. So,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

   

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=\frac{2}{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))
$$

The following table shows some values of a continuous function f(x) over the interval [2,12].

x 2 4 8 10 12
f(x) 5 3 2 1 1

Use the left Riemann sum, with the four subintervals indicated by the data, to approximate the area under the curve y=f(x) over the interval [2,12].

a
42
b
44
c
28
d
22
e
20
Don't Know
Submit

after.worked_solution:
In this case, we have $n=4$ rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

$$
A≈f(2)Δ{x}_{1}+f(4)Δ{x}_{2}+f(8)Δ{x}_{3}+f(10)Δ{x}_{4},
$$

where each $Δ{x}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $x$-value and the next one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i+1}-{x}_{i}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δx$'s.

| $x$ | $2$ | $4$ | $8$ | $10$ | $12$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δx$ | $2$ | $4$ | $2$ | $2$ | $-$ |
| $f(x)$ | $5$ | $3$ | $2$ | $1$ | $1$ |

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈5\cdot 2+3\cdot 4+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 2 \\  & =10+12+4+2 \\  & =28.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Using right endpoints, the sum is 4(3−0)+3(7−3)+5(12−7)+2(15−12)=12+12+25+6=55 customers.

after.worked_solution:
Let $A$ denote the area under the curve $y=C(t)$ over $[0,15].$ In this case, we have $n=4$ rectangles. Using the right Riemann sum, the area is approximated as 

$$
A≈C(3)Δ{t}_{1}+C(7)Δ{t}_{2}+C(12)Δ{t}_{3}+C(15)Δ{t}_{4},
$$

where each $Δ{t}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $t$-value and the previous one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{t}_{i}={t}_{i}-{t}_{i-1}.
$$

Find the value of the double sum

∑i=115∑j=1123ai(4−bj)

given that

∑i=115ai=30,∑j=112bj=45.

270

decision.explanation: Factor the double sum as 3(Σa_i)(Σ(4−b_j))=3·30·(4·12−45)=270. This tests double-sum algebra, absent from the supplied Linear Algebra topics, so it is prerequisite.

after.worked_solution:
The product rule for double summations states that

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{i}{b}_{j}={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{a}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{b}_{j}.
$$

So, using the product rule for double summations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}3{a}_{i}(4-{b}_{j}) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{15}3{a}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}(4-{b}_{j}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the rules for single summations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}3{a}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}(4-{b}_{j}) & =(3{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{a}_{i})\cdot ({\sum }_{j=1}^{12}4-{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}{b}_{j}) \\  & =(3{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{a}_{i})\cdot (4{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}1-{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}{b}_{j}) \\  & =(3\cdot 30)\cdot (4\cdot 12-45) \\  & =(90)\cdot (48-45) \\  & =(90)\cdot (3) \\  & =270\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the rules for single summations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{10}({a}_{i}-1){\sum }_{j=1}^{20}({b}_{j}+1) & =({\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{a}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{10}1)\cdot ({\sum }_{j=1}^{20}{b}_{j}+{\sum }_{j=1}^{20}1) \\  & =(12-10)\cdot (5+20) \\  & =(2)\cdot (25) \\  & =50.\end{aligned}
$$

Let P={z0,z1,…,zq} be a partition of the interval [1,5]. If Δzk=zk−zk−1, calculate ∑k=1q3Δzk.

decision.explanation: The sum telescopes: Σ3Δz_k=3(z_q−z_0)=3(5−1)=12. This tests interval partitions and telescoping sums, absent from the supplied Linear Algebra topics, so it is prerequisite.

after.worked_solution:
First, we take the factor $3$ outside the summation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}3Δ{z}_{k}=3{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}Δ{z}_{k}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that ${\sum }_{k=1}^{q}Δ{z}_{k}$ is just the length of the interval $[1,5],$ because

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}Δ{z}_{k} & =({z}_{1}-{z}_{0})+({z}_{2}-{z}_{1})+({z}_{3}-{z}_{2})+⋯+({z}_{q}-{z}_{q-1}) \\  & =(\cancel{{z}_{1}}-{z}_{0})+(\cancel{{z}_{2}}-\cancel{{z}_{1}})+(\cancel{{z}_{3}}-\cancel{{z}_{2}})+⋯+({z}_{q}-\cancel{{z}_{q-1}}) \\  & =-{z}_{0}+{z}_{q} \\  & ={z}_{q}-{z}_{0} \\  & =5-1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
3{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}Δ{z}_{k}=3\cdot 4=12.
$$

Therefore,

3∑k=1qΔzk=3⋅4=12.
